q: Pricing every bottle at the same multiple of its cost produces which distortion?
opts: The cheap end loses money and the expensive end subsidises it
Regional balance across the list collapses
Margins by the glass fall below margins by the bottle
The expensive end prices itself off the list
exp: Most lists slide the multiple downward as cost rises, so a fine bottle carries a larger cash margin at a smaller percentage. A flat multiple prices the best wines off the list, while the cheap end keeps its percentage and earns thin cash rather than a loss, and the expensive end, held to that same percentage, subsidises nothing below it.

q: Bringing their own bottle, a guest is charged for the glassware, the service and the lost sale. Name that charge.
exp: It is a policy rather than a rule, and it works best stated plainly on the list. Waiving it for a bottle the restaurant does not stock buys a great deal of goodwill.

q: Which single ratio, cost divided by selling price, does management watch to judge a beverage programme?
exp: It is read as a trend rather than as a target. A programme selling more fine wine at a lower percentage can be more profitable in cash than one hitting its number.

q: Recommending a bottle well below the price a table has named tends to produce what over a season?
opts: Trust, return visits and a larger total spend
An immediate loss the restaurant cannot recover
Guests who order nothing else for the rest of the meal
A reputation for a weak and cautious list
exp: Selling to a budget rather than above it is the durable strategy. A guest who feels worked over remembers that longer than they remember the wine.

q: Wines poured by the glass sit half-empty for days. Which gases are used to hold them?
exp: Argon is denser than air and blankets the surface, while nitrogen displaces the oxygen above the wine. Vacuum systems attack the same problem by removing the headspace.

q: A regular guest is visibly intoxicated and orders another bottle. What does the sommelier do?
opts: Decline the sale and offer food, water and a taxi
Serve it, since the guest is well known to the house
Serve a cheaper wine at the same price
Take the order and let the kitchen delay it
exp: Refusing service is a legal duty in most jurisdictions and a duty of care everywhere. Done courteously, quietly and without an audience, it rarely costs the relationship.

q: Asked about a wine they genuinely do not know, which response serves the guest best?
opts: Improvise a plausible description from the region and grape
Steer the conversation toward a wine they do know
Say so, then find out and come back with a real answer
Hand over the list and let the guest decide alone
exp: Guests forgive not knowing and remember being misled. The recovery, made quickly, usually reads as more expert than a smooth invention would.

q: Which French term names the trolley or side table used for finishing and serving beside the guest?
exp: Decanting, carving and flaming all happen there rather than on the guest's own table. It keeps the work visible without putting equipment among the plates.

q: One glass of a 1990 first growth is wanted with the rest of the bottle left intact. Which device makes that possible?
exp: A fine needle passes through the cork, argon replaces what is drawn out, and the cork reseals behind it. It changed which bottles a list can sensibly open.

q: Which phrase describes service that meets a need before the guest has voiced it?
exp: Water refilled unasked, a glass changed before the next wine arrives, a chair steadied. It is the difference between a table being served and a table being looked after.

q: Drawing a new ward onto the Wine of Origin map takes evidence a new district never has to produce. What must the applicants demonstrate?
opts: That at least ten registered producers already make and bottle wine inside the proposed boundary
A distinct soil, climate and ecology in the ground itself
That the area lies wholly within a single registered estate
That the proposed name has a documented history of use on labels going back fifty years
exp: A district can follow broad geography and even administrative convenience, but the ward is the scheme's terroir tier and its boundary has to be argued from the land. That is why a ward name like Groenekloof carries real information on a label: it is a claim about the ground, not about a map-maker's tidiness.

q: Records alone cannot win a Cape wine its certification seal. What must the wine itself get through before the seal is granted?
opts: A blind tasting panel and laboratory analysis
A ballot of its district's producers
Six months of maturation in tank or barrel before bottling
A vineyard inspection at harvest
exp: Every certified wine is chemically analysed and tasted blind by the Wine and Spirit Board's panels, and a faulty wine fails whatever its paperwork says. The seal is therefore a statement about the liquid as well as the ledger, which is not true of every origin system in the world.

q: Europe's appellation idea reached the Cape as law in the early 1970s, and one vintage was the first sold under Wine of Origin seals. Give the year.
exp: The scheme was promulgated in 1972 and certified its first wines with the 1973 harvest, which makes it one of the oldest origin systems outside Europe. It borrowed the layered idea of place from the French model while refusing the link between place and permitted grape: a Cape origin says where the fruit grew, and nothing else.

q: One producer, one cellar, and a flagship blend drawing on vineyards forty kilometres apart. Which label claim has the distance cost that wine?
exp: An estate wine must come off land farmed as one contiguous unit, with the wine made in a cellar standing on that unit, so scattered vineyards disqualify the words however good the farming. The claim is about unity of place and production, not quality: a second farm across the valley, or any bought-in fruit, bars a wine that may still be the best in the country.

q: Climbing from the Swartland's rolling grain country to a fold-mountain summit crosses the winelands' three great rocks in a single walk. In what order?
opts: Granite in the low hills, shale across the middle slopes, sandstone capping the top
Shale in the low hills, granite on the middle slopes, sandstone at the top
Sandstone in the low hills, granite on the middle slopes, shale at the top
Shale in the low hills, sandstone across the middle slopes, granite forming the summit
exp: The low country is shale ground, the domes and foot slopes - Paarl Mountain, the Paardeberg, the lower flanks of the Simonsberg - are granite, and the sandstone caps the peaks. Soils creep downhill, so a foot-slope block often farms a mixture of all three, which is one reason Cape growers name the rock rather than the topsoil.

q: Every other rock in the winelands is younger than the one the whole Cape stands on, an ocean-floor mud pressed hard more than half a billion years ago. Name it.
exp: The Malmesbury Group is Precambrian sediment, hardened before the first shelled creatures existed, and everything else under the vineyards is dramatically younger. It weathers to deep red-brown clay hills that hold winter rain well, and its sheer age is part of why Cape soils run so leached and naturally low in vigour.
